Silly-Things.title: Silly Things
Silly-Things.content:
There are 1000 strings that are different demonware urls. Why… Each of them is like 24 ish characters. So they threw away 24-25 kB for fun.
That’s not even counting the huge number of “dw/err” or “dw/info” or “dw/warn”
Entirety of the periodic table… 3x times.
“Silly Lobby Name”…
They have several debug error messages everywhere. Some have an exclamation point. This one is apparently worse than most
smosUpdate - sceSifSendCmd failed to queue !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

That’s a lot of exclamation points. All jokes aside, that would not be a very good message to get… the Sif is how the EE (think northbridge) and the IOP (basically the PS2’s southbridge, but like only slower peripherals) communicated. That includes like the controllers and stuff. Bad.

Introduction
Hey!
This is a project I’m working on in my free time, to learn more about Outrun 2006: Coast 2 Coast’s internals, and to have fun doing it. It’s a game I grew up playing with my Dad and siblings a lot, and so I have a lot of good memories.
It’s still in early stages. If you have any comments or questions, including some files for importing the labels and symbols I’ve already created into Ghidra, shoot me a discord message at thereal_ethanhunt and I’m sure we can figure it out.
Keep in mind, I have no idea what version of the game I’m working with. It’s one of the US versions (I have no idea if there are more than one version?), but we dumped the iso a few years ago, and then the games “dropped off the back of a truck” in a move like two years ago. We think someone stole it and our xbox 360… I guess it was our mistake for writing “Playstation Games” and “XBox” on the side of the boxes. Hopefuly they didn’t throw it away at least.

logs/2026-03-16.content:
RE Daily: 2026-03-16
So I’m running into a pretty major roadblock. It was the reason I didn’t end up doing a log yesterday… I’m just really pounding my head against this.
So the main binary is sorta sorted into 3 big chunks of memory. You have memory at like 0x00100000-0x00400000. That’s like most of the globals and all of the functions, and a decent number of strings.
Then you have data starting at 0x20100000 and at 0x30200000. This is where things get funky. A ton of functions have no references Ghidra can find. Like probably a third or so. Except there are references, in these big tables in those two regions. I think, based on the structure, they’re almost all class functions with like Vtables and stuff that take a “this” pointer.
Edit!~~~~
I’m just a goober! I wrote all this stuff complaining, and literally 15 minutes later I had the thought to look at a PS2 memory map. Sigh, I’m sorta an idiot sometimes.
So it turns out that the Emotion Engine memory map (the part we care about, at least) looks like this:






























TitleStartEndRAM0x00Idk, 24 MBRAM (uncached)0x200000000x21e847ffRAM (Uncached and accelerated)0x301000000x31f847ff(Really, the uncached and uncached accelerated versions aren’t that long… It does have an MMU so it’s nice to have as much of the virtual address as you need that you can move around tho)
Anyway, the idea is that with the uncached, it’s good for pieces of memory that you use DMA on and stuff. The EE has caches and stuff, so if you like read from a piece of memory, and then the DMA overwrites it, and you try to do a normal read on it, you’ll get the cached version, not the new version. The uncached is like that, except that writes are cached with what’s called a writeback buffer, just not reads. That can be dangerous if another chip is gonna read what you wrote, but you’re a game developer (well, probably not, but the person programming this was) so you’re smart enough not to do something dumb, like this here reverse engineer!
Anyway, so all of the data in uncached RAM and uncached/accelerated RAM is the same! Like it’s different ways of accessing the same location. Technically, with the memory mapping feature, Ghidra is supposed to handle this automatically… But I couldn’t figure it out, so I wrote a python script to copy everything down from the other two types to the main ram.
After that, I spent a long time working on mapping the class structure. I put together 24 class constructors today in Ghidra, along with the requisite structs and stuff. Ghidra can handle object oriented code, it’s just a little groaty to do, and very hard work on my end. But we’re down to like only like 100 or so unreferenced functions, and those are probably just stuck in VTables I haven’t gotten to yet.
I am learning an awful lot about C++ classes under the hood. And holy cow, does this game have a ton of subclasses. I’m gonna need to figure out a way to start labeling them all better, since this currently stinks!

logs/2026-03-17.content:
RE Daily: 2026-03-17
I’m still mapping out classes. And the annoying thing is it just feels like lots of busywork, ish. I’m still trying to decide if I want to write a script to automate some of this. I think my only concern is, at least for now, it feels simple enough to not be interesting, but different enough to make me concerned about just automating it. So far we’re up to 34 classes, and the deepest nest I found was 4 deep (layers of inheritance). And some of these classes are massive!
I really hope this is GUI classes. Because if they’re using this many nested classes for game code, I’m going to have words with the software architecture guy.

logs/2026-03-18.content:
RE Daily: 2026-03-18
Well, I’ve decided I’ve had enough with classes for now. I’ve currently made 43 classes, and I just can’t anymore, for now at least. So I’mma go back to stuff that actually looks like C for a bit.
Mostly, I just relabeled a lot of things
I also realized something interesting! I think the files on disk are being used as like, virtual directories or something. I think this since we see a lot of fopen calls to like “Scripts/bin/req_****”. And I was like “wait a minute there’s no directories.”
Unfortunately, I’m sorta dumb and for a sec, I was like “oh I bet there’s one file that stores that whole virtual file system.” Until I realized that Scripts.ps2 was a file. So it looks like “directories” are files with entries.
It’s also interesting how they store them. Best I can tell, the file names are hashed, and the filename hash for whatever you’re asking for is generated at runtime. They also might be doing the “subdirectories” as like recursive reads into those files, who knows. I need to spend a few more minutes on it.
The files themselves are also interesting.
There’s this function, I’m like 90% certain of what it does but the question mark stays on, that I call
load_file_into_mem?("\\Scripts\\bin\\RaceAssignment.bin",0x62ace0,0,0);
DAT_0036fd20 = get_property_from_loaded_file?("RACE_MAPPING_ARRAY",(int *)&DAT_0062ace0);
I’m not quite sure what it returns, but it does return something. Maybe a file pointer, but I feel like a function like this should “clean-up” after itself since it calls open internally. Who knows. I’ve only like half reversed engineered it, mostly just guessing. And calls to this function are always followed by that “get_property_from_loaded_file?” function. It does some hash comparison of the key (there might be a better word for it) with the file in a loop, probably looking through a hashed header, and then a binary search for something. I think it returns a pointer to where in the file the given data-structure you’re asking for is? Still working through it, or maybe I’ll move on for now since I’m pretty sure what it does on the high-level. Anyway, it’s cool that they have a pretty developed, high-level system these file-system, and parsing files in a pretty clever robust way. As I’ve said before, the more I’ve dug through their folder, the more I think these guys are pros… mostly. Except for saving memory. Still bad at that.
